free-energy-equilibrium-s1.title: Five reactions at 298 K
free-energy-equilibrium-s1.text: Standard free energy changes for five reactions, A to E, all at 298 K. R = 8.314 J/(mol·K).

table.caption: ΔG° of five reactions at 298 K
Three equilibria and their K values at 298 K

items.q: For which reaction is K closest to 1?
options: A
C
E
B

why.correct: ΔG° = −RT ln K. When ΔG° = 0, ln K = 0 and K = 1.
options: ΔG° = −20.0 kJ/mol gives K of about 3 × 10³, far above 1.
Right: ΔG° = 0 gives ln K = 0, so K = 1.
ΔG° = +20.0 kJ/mol gives K of about 3 × 10⁻⁴, far below 1.
ΔG° = −5.0 kJ/mol gives K of about 7.5: close-ish, but not as close as reaction C.

items.q: Calculate K for reaction A at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used ΔG° in kJ with R in J. Convert −20.0 kJ/mol to −20,000 J/mol.
Value: you raised 10 to the power instead of e. ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log, so K = e^(−ΔG°/RT).
Sign: −ΔG°/RT = −(−20,000)/(8.314 × 298) = +8.07, a positive exponent, so K > 1.

why.correct: ln K = −ΔG°/RT = −(−20,000 J/mol)/[(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K)] = 8.072. K = e^8.072 = 3.2 × 10³ (two significant figures). K > 1, as expected for ΔG° < 0.

items.q: At equilibrium, which reaction has mostly reactants and very little product?
options: A
C
D
E

why.correct: The more positive ΔG°, the smaller K, and the more the equilibrium mixture is reactants.
options: ΔG° < 0 gives K > 1: products are favored.
K = 1: neither side is strongly favored, so both are present in large amounts.
K ≈ 0.13: reactants are favored, but much less strongly than in reaction E.
Right: ΔG° = +20.0 kJ/mol gives K ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴, so reactants are favored.

items.q: A student says reaction D, with ΔG° = +5.0 kJ/mol, "cannot happen at all." Which reply is best?
options: K ≈ 0.13, so from pure reactants some product forms until Q = K.
The student is right, because a reaction with ΔG° > 0 makes no product.
The reaction goes to completion, because ΔG° is so close to zero.
The reaction happens once a catalyst is added, which makes ΔG° negative.

why.correct: ΔG° refers to standard conditions. A positive value means K < 1: reactants are favored at equilibrium, but some product is still present.
options: Right: a positive ΔG° means K < 1, not K = 0. An equilibrium mixture still contains product.
ΔG° > 0 means K < 1. Starting from reactants, Q = 0 < K, so the net reaction goes forward a little.
Close to zero means K is close to 1, not that the reaction goes to completion.
A catalyst does not change ΔG° or K.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° for the ionization of acetic acid at 298 K.

mistakes.why: Value: you used log instead of ln. ΔG° = −RT ln K uses the natural log.
Sign: ln(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) is negative, so −RT ln K is positive.
Units: R in J/(mol·K) gives J/mol. Divide by 1000 to report kJ/mol.

why.correct: ΔG° = −RT ln K = −(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K) ln(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = −(2477.6)(−10.925) = 2.71 × 10⁴ J/mol = 27 kJ/mol (two significant figures, from K).

items.q: Which equilibrium has a negative ΔG°?
options: The ionization of acetic acid
The dissociation of N₂O₄
The formation of NH₃
No equilibrium in the table, since at equilibrium ΔG° = 0

why.correct: K > 1 ⇔ ΔG° < 0. Only the ammonia synthesis has K > 1.
options: K = 0.15 < 1, so ΔG° > 0 (about +4.7 kJ/mol).
Right: K = 6.6 × 10⁵ > 1, so ln K > 0 and ΔG° < 0.
At equilibrium ΔG (not ΔG°) is zero. ΔG° is a fixed value set by K.

items.q: Calculate ΔG° at 298 K for 2 NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g).

mistakes.why: Sign: this is the reverse of the reaction in the table, so K = 1/0.15 = 6.7 and ΔG° is negative.

why.correct: Reversing the reaction inverts K: K = 1/0.15 = 6.67. ΔG° = −(8.314)(298) ln(6.67) = −4.70 × 10³ J/mol = -4.7 kJ/mol. (Equivalently, flip the sign of ΔG° for the forward reaction.)

items.q: A flask of N₂O₄ and NO₂ at 298 K has Q = 0.010. Which statement is correct?
options: ΔG° is positive, so NO₂ can form after the flask is heated, not before.
Q < K, so the net reaction forms more N₂O₄ until Q rises to K.
Q < K, so ΔG is negative now and the net reaction forms more NO₂.
K changes to 0.010 to match the flask, so there is no net reaction.

why.correct: Whether a mixture reacts forward depends on Q compared with K. Q = 0.010 < K = 0.15, so the net reaction goes forward even though ΔG° > 0.
options: ΔG° describes standard conditions. Here Q < K, so the net forward reaction is favored now.
Forming N₂O₄ would lower Q further. To raise Q, NO₂ must form.
Right: ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q is negative when Q < K, so the mixture moves toward products.
K changes only with temperature; it stays 0.15 here.

items.q: For N₂(g) + 3 H₂(g) ⇌ 2 NH₃(g), ΔG° = −33.2 kJ/mol at 298 K. Calculate K. (R = 8.314 J/(mol·K))

mistakes.why: Value: ΔG° must be in J/mol to match R: −33,200 J/mol.
Sign: −ΔG°/RT = +13.4, so K is large, not small.

why.correct: ln K = −ΔG°/RT = 33,200 J/mol ÷ [(8.314 J/(mol·K))(298 K)] = 13.40. K = e^13.40 = 6.6 × 10⁵ (two significant figures). The large K matches the strongly negative ΔG°.

items.q: A gas-phase reaction has K = 20.2 at 400. K. Calculate ΔG° at 400. K, in kJ/mol.

mistakes.why: Value: you used 298 K. Use the temperature at which K was measured: 400. K.
Value: 400. K is already in kelvin; do not subtract 273.
Value: use ln, not log, in ΔG° = −RT ln K.

items.q: If ΔG° for a reaction is large and negative, what is true of K?
options: K is much greater than 1, so products are favored at equilibrium.
K is much less than 1, so reactants are favored at equilibrium.
K is equal to 1, so equal amounts of reactants and products are present.
K is negative, because ΔG° is negative.

why.correct: K = e^(−ΔG°/RT). A large negative ΔG° gives a large positive exponent and K ≫ 1.
options: Right: ln K = −ΔG°/RT is large and positive.
That is the case for a large positive ΔG°.
K = 1 goes with ΔG° = 0.
K is an exponential, e^(−ΔG°/RT), so it is positive whatever the sign of ΔG°.

items.q: Reaction 1 has ΔG° = −5.70 kJ/mol and K₁ = 9.98 at 298 K. Reaction 2 is reaction 1 multiplied by 2. What are ΔG° and K for reaction 2?
options: ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol and K = 20.0
ΔG° = −5.70 kJ/mol and K = 99.6
ΔG° = −2.85 kJ/mol and K = 3.16
ΔG° = −11.4 kJ/mol and K = 99.6

why.correct: ΔG° scales with the coefficients; since ΔG° = −RT ln K, doubling ΔG° doubles ln K, which squares K.
options: Doubling the reaction squares K; it does not double it. Check: −RT ln K must equal −11.4 kJ/mol.
ΔG° is extensive: twice the reaction releases twice the free energy.
That halves the reaction. Multiplying by 2 doubles ΔG°.
Right: doubling a reaction doubles ΔG° and squares K (9.98² = 99.6).

items.q: A reaction mixture is at equilibrium. Which statement is correct?
options: ΔG° is zero, because nothing in the mixture is changing.
ΔG for the system is zero, while ΔG° keeps its fixed value set by K.
ΔG is negative, because the forward reaction is still running.
K equals zero, because the reaction has stopped.

why.correct: ΔG measures the drive under the actual conditions; it is zero at equilibrium. ΔG° refers to standard conditions and is fixed for a given T.
options: ΔG° is the standard value and equals −RT ln K; it is zero only when K = 1.
Right: at equilibrium Q = K and ΔG = 0; ΔG° = −RT ln K does not change.
Forward and reverse rates are equal, so there is no net drive in either direction: ΔG = 0.
The reaction has not stopped (it is dynamic), and K is a fixed positive number.

items.q: For a reaction at 298 K, ΔG° = +0.5 kJ/mol. Which description of the equilibrium mixture is best?
options: K ≈ 0.8, close to 1, so both reactants and products are abundant.
K is very small, so the mixture is nearly pure reactants.
K is very large, so the reaction goes nearly to completion.
K is 0.5, the same number as ΔG° in kJ/mol.

why.correct: When ΔG° is near zero, K is near 1 and reactants and products are both present in significant amounts.
options: Right: e^(−500/2477.6) = 0.82. With ΔG° near zero, neither side dominates.
A small positive ΔG° gives K slightly below 1, not a very small K.
A large K needs a large negative ΔG°.
K comes from e^(−ΔG°/RT), not from ΔG° itself.

items.q: A reaction has ΔH° < 0 and ΔS° < 0, so ΔG° becomes less negative as T rises. The temperature is raised from 300 K to 400 K. Predict the change in each quantity.

variables.name: ΔG° of the reaction
variables.why: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS°; with ΔS° < 0, −TΔS° is positive and grows with T, so ΔG° rises (becomes less negative).

variables.name: K of the reaction
variables.why: A less negative ΔG° gives a smaller −ΔG°/RT, so K falls; this matches Le Châtelier for an exothermic reaction.

variables.name: The value of R used in ΔG° = −RT ln K
variables.why: R is a constant, 8.314 J/(mol·K), at every temperature.

why.correct: For an exothermic reaction with ΔS° < 0, heating raises ΔG° and lowers K.

items.q: Which set of units makes ΔG° = −RT ln K come out in J/mol?
options: R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K) and T in K
R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in °C
R = 8.314 J/(mol·K) and T in K
R = 8.314 kJ/(mol·K) and T in K

why.correct: Use the energy form of R, 8.314 J/(mol·K), with T in kelvin. Divide by 1000 for kJ/mol.
options: That R is for gas laws; it gives L·atm/mol, not J/mol.
Temperature must be in kelvin.
Right: J/(mol·K) × K = J/mol; ln K has no units.
R is 8.314 J/(mol·K); in kJ it is 0.008314 kJ/(mol·K).
